# Misfire on Cyl 2 & 3, but doesn't (exactly) match TSB

If you are staring at a 2009 Honda Accord with persistent DTCs P0302 and P0303 but no accompanying P0339, you have likely already ruled out the most common culprits. You've swapped ignition coils, replaced spark plugs, hunted for intake manifold leaks, and even used a jump box to verify battery health. The fact that the engine runs perfectly for a few seconds after startup before the misfire codes reappear suggests a transition from an open-loop state to closed-loop operation, but the symptoms don't align perfectly with Technical Service Bulletin 09-050.

TSB 09-050 specifically addresses issues where the crankshaft position sensor signal becomes erratic or drops out entirely, often resulting in a P0339 code alongside misfires. The absence of that specific code indicates the ECU is still receiving valid crankshaft revolution data, even if it is struggling to time ignition events correctly during warm-up. This distinction is critical because it points away from a hard sensor failure and toward a timing synchronization issue or a fuel delivery problem that manifests only once the lambda sensors take control.

The behavior you are describingâperfect idle for 30 seconds followed by illumination of the check engine lightâis classic open-loop to closed-loop transition syndrome. When the car starts, the ECU operates in open loop, ignoring the oxygen sensors and running a fixed fuel map based on coolant temperature and throttle position. As soon as the upstream O2 sensor (usually located before the catalytic converter) detects that the exhaust is within a certain range, the ECU switches to closed loop. At this moment, it begins adjusting the fuel trim to maintain a stoichiometric air-fuel ratio of 14.7:1.

If there is a vacuum leak, the ECU will attempt to compensate by enriching the mixture. If that compensation exceeds the mechanical limits of the injectors or if the leak is large enough to overwhelm the sensor's ability to report accurately, the system enters a "limp" mode where it can no longer correct the air-fuel ratio. This often triggers misfire codes because the lean condition causes cylinder combustion instability. The simultaneous illumination of the VSA (Vehicle Stability Assist) light alongside the engine light is a secondary safety measure; modern ECUs monitor drivability parameters and will disable stability control features if they detect erratic firing patterns that could destabilize the vehicle.

Before you hand over significant funds for a scan tool reprogramming or an ECU replacement, consider the possibility of a failing fuel pressure regulator or a clogged fuel filter that restricts flow under load but appears fine at idle. When the engine is cold, volumetric efficiency is lower, and the demand on the fuel system is minimal. Once the coolant sensor indicates the engine is warm enough to close the loop, the ECU demands precise fuel delivery. If the regulator cannot maintain pressure or the filter is restricting flow, the resulting lean condition triggers the misfires only after the threshold for closed-loop operation is crossed.

Another potential pitfall in diagnosing this specific scenario is overlooking the ignition coil pack's internal resistance characteristics. While swapping coils often resolves issues caused by a single bad unit, if one of the new coils has slightly higher impedance than the others, it might function adequately during the high-voltage burst of open-loop startup but fail to sustain spark under the precise timing requirements of closed-loop operation. Ensure the replacement parts are OEM or high-quality equivalents, as aftermarket variations can introduce subtle timing delays that manifest as misfires only under specific load conditions.

If these steps do not yield results and the issue persists strictly during the closed-loop transition, the diagnosis may indeed involve the crankshaft position sensor circuit. While TSB 09-050 covers this, your lack of a P0339 code means the failure mode is likely different from the documented case. In such instances, some mechanics have found success by cleaning the electrical connector on the sensor or re-seating it to ensure consistent contact resistance. However, if the sensor itself is degrading in a way that causes signal noise without dropping out completely, the ECU might interpret this as a misfire rather than a sensor fault.

If you find yourself needing to verify complex engine management behaviors beyond standard diagnostic tools, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can occasionally provide insights into how modern automotive architectures handle error states and fail-safes, though specific hardware diagnostics usually require proprietary equipment. The decision to replace the ECU should be a last resort; without water intrusion or known internal component failure, reprogramming rarely fixes mechanical or electrical marginality issues in this generation of Honda engines.
